title: Copy a reference assembly onto a turned fixture
instruction: Use the three loose blocks to build a copy of the glued model on the empty white plate. Place each block relative to this plate's red edge as its twin sits relative to the model plate's red edge, within 8 mm and 10 degrees.
context: Spacecraft hardware is built to its drawings. On the integration bench a technician often also has a physical reference beside the build, such as a pathfinder assembly or the engineering model, and checks the build against it: which part goes where, which sits on which, and which way each one faces. The two fixtures are not always set up facing the same way, so the match is read against a datum edge, not the room. Aircraft and spacecraft structure and systems assemblers (O*NET 51-2011) do this kind of bench work every day. Here the robot has to read a glued three-block model through its own cameras, including which block sits on which and which way each one runs, then rebuild it from loose twins on a second plate that is turned 90 degrees, registered to that plate's red datum edge within 8 mm and 10 degrees. The cube can go on only after the base, so the build order is forced. Unlike copying a structure from a picture, the reference is a solid object in the scene and the copy is measured in a turned datum frame, so a copy that only looks alike earns little: a copy made in the room's orientation, or with the datum reversed, scores 0; a copy mirrored end for end along the red edge earns 0.33, and one mirrored toward and away from the red edge scores 0. A 1 g tabletop analogue of bench integration work; no microgravity is claimed.
setup: Station table; the left arm does the work and the right arm is idle at its ready pose. Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, heights above the table top; the left arm's base is at y = +0.305. All objects are rigid and matte with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). The plates are wood or acrylic; the six blocks are pine or PLA printed at about 50% infill. Fixed: two identical plates, each a white (sRGB 0.92, 0.92, 0.90) top 140 x 140 x 10 mm with a red (sRGB 0.80, 0.12, 0.10) datum strip 15 x 140 x 10 mm flush along one edge, so 155 x 140 mm overall and 10 mm tall. The model plate's white top is centred at (0.260, -0.040), spanning x 0.190 to 0.330 and y -0.110 to 0.030, with its red strip along the far edge (x 0.330 to 0.345). The empty plate's white top is centred at (0.240, 0.190), spanning x 0.170 to 0.310 and y 0.120 to 0.260, with its red strip along the outboard edge (y 0.260 to 0.275), so it is turned 90 degrees to the model plate; the plates are 90 mm apart. The model, three blocks glued to the model plate and to each other: a blue (sRGB 0.15, 0.35, 0.80) base block 100 x 40 x 30 mm (long, wide, tall) lying on a 100 x 40 face with its long axis along y, centred at (0.225, -0.040), so it spans y -0.090 to 0.010; an orange (sRGB 0.90, 0.45, 0.10) cube of 40 mm on top of the base's +y end, centred at (0.225, -0.010), flush with that end and with both long faces of the base; a green (sRGB 0.20, 0.60, 0.30) side block 60 x 30 x 40 mm standing on a 60 x 30 face with its long axis along x, centred at (0.285, -0.075), spanning x 0.255 to 0.315 and y -0.090 to -0.060, so its outer face is flush with the base's -y end, it stands 10 mm clear of the base's far face and its far end is 15 mm short of the red strip. In each plate's own frame (origin at the centre of the white top, u toward the red strip, v 90 degrees to the left of u as seen facing the strip) the model is: base centre (u, v) = (-35, 0) mm, long axis along v; cube centre (-35, +30) mm, on the base; side block centre (+25, -35) mm, long axis along u. Loose, the three twins of the model blocks, the same sizes and colours, standing on the table outboard of the empty plate: the blue base block, 70 g, lying on a 100 x 40 face (30 mm tall) with its long axis along y, centred at (0.330, 0.395); the green side block, 45 g, standing on a 60 x 30 face (40 mm tall) with its long axis along x, centred at (0.225, 0.415); the orange cube, 40 g, centred at (0.140, 0.400), faces square to the table edges. The loose blocks are at least 35 mm apart edge to edge and at least 70 mm from the empty plate's red strip. Built correctly, the copy on the empty plate has the base centred at (0.240, 0.155) with its long axis along x, the cube on its near end at (0.210, 0.155) and the side block centred at (0.275, 0.215) with its long axis along y, its near end 10 mm outboard of the base's long side and its far face flush with the base's far end. To build it: two 155 x 140 mm boards 10 mm thick (wood or acrylic), painted white with the last 15 mm along one 140 mm edge painted red, taped to the table at the stated positions; six blocks cut from pine or printed in PLA at about 50% infill to size, three glued in place on the model plate, the loose ones made to the stated masses.
scoring: End state only, judged on the empty plate from a top photo, a side photo and a tape measure, in that plate's own frame (origin at the centre of its 140 x 140 mm white top, u toward its red strip, v to the left as seen facing the strip). Each block's place is where its glued twin sits in the model plate's frame: base centre (u, v) = (-35, 0) mm with its long axis along v, standing on the plate; side block centre (+25, -35) mm with its long axis along u, standing on the plate; cube centre (-35, +30) mm, standing on the base. A place takes only its own block, matched by size and colour. A loose block is in place when it is at rest (under 10 mm/s), flat (its height axis within 5 degrees of vertical, either way up: the base on a 100 x 40 mm face, the side block on a 60 x 30 mm face, the cube on any face), its lowest point within 4 mm of the plate's top (base, side block) or of the base's top, 30 mm above the plate (cube), its centre within 8 mm of its place, and its long axis within 10 degrees of its place's axis, either way round (the cube's faces within 10 degrees of square to the plate's edges). Score: 1/3 for each block in place, the base, the side block and the cube, except that the cube counts only when the base is also in place, since the cube's place is on the base and a side block lying on a long face is also 30 mm tall; so 0, 0.33, 0.67 or 1.0. The start state, a copy built in the room's orientation instead of the datum's, a copy built with the red strip reversed and a copy mirrored toward and away from the red strip all score 0; a copy mirrored end for end along the red strip earns 0.33, for the base. A base on its side or off its place by more than 8 mm or 10 degrees earns nothing for itself or for the cube on it. A side block pushed against the base is 10 mm off its place and earns nothing for that block; so do a side block lying on a long face or standing on end, and a cube on the plate, on the wrong end of the base or turned 45 degrees. A block still moving or held earns nothing. Success, which ends the trial, is all three blocks in place and still for 1 s. In simulation every horizontal and angle test uses the block's centre and quaternion, not its axis-aligned bounds; the bottom height is the block's lowest point; an exact 8.0 mm offset counts (0.1 mm epsilon), and so does an exact 10.0 degrees. The plates and the model are fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which either plate or any model block moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand the three loose blocks back on their marks: the base long axis across the table, the side block long axis forward, the cube square to the table edges; the plates and the glued model do not move.
fidelity: Approximate: rigid blocks and plates sharing one matte material (friction 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic); the blocks stand in for the units of a model, so there are no fasteners, connectors, alignment pins or adhesive, and nothing is fixed after placing; the red strip stands in for a datum edge; the loose blocks are light (40 to 70 g) to suit the arm. The model and the plates cannot move. Earth gravity on a bench, which is also where this work is done. In simulation, release is inferred from the blocks being at rest, so a block held motionless in place would also count; the real-world rule, judged after the gripper has opened and moved clear, closes that gap.
